summary: Austria is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, more than 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorization is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90. Longer stays run through the national Visa D or a residence title such as the Red-White-Red Card.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says credit cards are widely accepted at main hotels, shops and restaurants, but smaller establishments may only accept cash.

safety.text: The UK government says crime levels are generally low, but there are higher levels of petty crime, particularly pickpocketing, in the big city centres and in city parks after dark. roadVignette.text: Austrian motorways and expressways may only be used with a valid vignette — either the digital one tied to your number plate or the traditional sticker, which ASFINAG is selling for the last time in 2026. The Alpine section tolls (A9 Gleinalm and Bosruck, A10 Tauern and Katschberg, A11 Karawanken, A13 Brenner, S16 Arlberg) are charged separately on top of the vignette.

source.name: ASFINAG — Vignette rates 2026

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Austria: the Schengen Borders Code counts stays on the territory of all the Member States together.
Driving on Austrian motorways requires a vignette (€12.80 for 10 days, €106.80 for a year; digital or sticker). ASFINAG charges a €200 substitute toll for a car or camper van without one.
Once ETIAS starts, the EU says applications are made on the official ETIAS website or the official ETIAS mobile app; it is not yet in operation.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Austria?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Austria and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does an Austria Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries. Austria's national Visa D costs €195 (€97 for children under 6) under the Fees Act.

faq.question: What is Austria's Red-White-Red Card?
faq.answer: It is an Austrian residence and work title for non-EU workers. On the skilled-workers-in-shortage-occupations route, migration.gv.at says eligibility is assessed on points, the card is generally issued for 24 months, it entitles you to work for the employer named in the application, and the application fee is €218.

faq.question: Do I need a vignette to drive in Austria?
faq.answer: Yes. All motorways and expressways require a vignette: €12.80 for 10 days, €32 for 2 months or €106.80 for a year (2026 car prices), as a sticker or digital vignette. Driving without one means paying a €200 substitute toll on the spot.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Austria without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area.
